common_name: Chief of Chiefs Louisiana Iris (Rosy-Orange and Rust Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: New Orleans hybridizer Patrick O'Connor registered Chief of Chiefs in 2008 from a cross of two of his own earlier introductions, 'Lemon Zest' and 'Bellocq,' producing a warm rosy-orange-edged standard over a pale yellow, darker-veined center, with cream style arms washed rose at the tips and rust-orange falls carrying a bold orange-yellow thumbprint signal overlaid by a gold line. Blooming midseason on well-branched 34-inch stalks, it combines the ruffled form typical of modern Louisiana hybrids with an unusually warm color range for the class, which runs heavily toward blues, purples, and reds. Site it in full sun with rich, constantly moist to wet soil typical of Louisiana iris culture, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to sustain vigor.
sources: Garden Club of Houston Bulb & Plant Mart plant notes

common_name: Faubourg-Saint John Louisiana Iris (Reddish-Purple Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Registered by New Orleans hybridizer Patrick O'Connor in 2001 from a cross of 'Helen Naish' and 'False River,' Faubourg-Saint John bears heavily ruffled reddish-purple flowers with a yellow, crown-shaped signal on the falls and reddish-purple style arms washed with a greenish-cream base, on well-branched 34-inch stalks blooming midseason. O'Connor named it for the historic Faubourg St. John neighborhood along Bayou St. John in New Orleans, and later used a self-cross of the cultivar onto itself to breed the award-winning 'German Coast.' Grow it in full sun with rich, constantly moist to wet soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.
